speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our system would be undermined if criminals were to abuse our system to carry out illicit activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To this end, Singapore has taken a resolute stance against money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These three strategies are also used to combat terrorism financing and proliferation financing; (b) continuously reviewing our processes and updating our laws to ensure that they remain effective and in line with international standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To this end, Singapore has been an active member of the Financial Action Task Force, or FATF for short, since 1992.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The FATF sets the international standards for tackling money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore has been assessed by the FATF to have a strong legal and institutional framework and we are determined to maintain our good standing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill is in line with the Government's consistent approach, as it seeks to strengthen our international cooperation regime and framework for trusts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are two main components to this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, Singapore's international criminal cooperation regime will be updated to ensure it remains efficient, effective and in line with international standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will enhance our ability to cooperate with other jurisdictions to combat crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, the Trustees Act will be updated to better support Singapore's legal regime by revising the trustees' obligations and imposing effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will take hon Members through these two components of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, let me begin with the changes to the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, or MACMA for short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Mutual legal assistance is a process where states seek and provide assistance to one another for the purposes of criminal investigations, prosecution and other proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A strong international cooperation framework is especially vital in our world today, as crime is increasingly transnational in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In this regard, it is in our interests to ensure that our laws are updated to allow us to cooperate effectively with other countries to prevent and punish crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We, however, do not rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill will further improve our processes and capabilities to assist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will highlight four key amendments that the Bill will make to the MACMA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the Bill will empower our law enforcement authorities to take statements from persons for the purposes of assisting foreign criminal investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, section 21 of the MACMA requires that criminal proceedings have commenced in the foreign country before a witness may be compelled to give evidence to aid in those proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This generally means that prosecution must have been initiated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As such, if the foreign country is still investigating and has yet to commence proceedings, then Singapore would be unable to assist with the taking of evidence under section 21 of the MACMA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In contrast, our domestic authorities are empowered, under our Criminal Procedure Code, to take statements from persons for the purpose of domestic investigations, before the matter reaches our courts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A new section 21A will address this issue to ensure that powers available for domestic authorities are also available for use in response to requests for mutual legal assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will add to our current powers, which pertain to property "used" in the commission of such offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This expands the scope of property covered under the MACMA and strengthens our ability to deprive criminals of their property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in line with FATF's definition of "criminal property", which covers instrumentalities used and intended for use in money laundering and other offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, the Bill will clarify when foreign proceedings are deemed concluded for the purposes of enforcement of a foreign confiscation order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: While the MACMA already contains examples of when proceedings are considered concluded, such as discontinuance of proceedings or acquittal, the Bill will further clarify that proceedings are concluded when there is no right of appeal following the acquittal, for example, or that all rights of appeal have expired or are exhausted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This clarifies a grey area in determining when proceedings are concluded, such as where the defendant has been acquitted but the foreign state is still pursuing an appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A foreign confiscation order is an order made in connection with the foreign offence for the recovery, forfeiture or confiscation of any payment or property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, we can only enforce foreign confiscation orders made in judicial proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A number of jurisdictions, especially those with civil law systems, have confiscation orders which may be issued by an authority other than a Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There is thus a need to take a broader approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also contains other technical amendments, all intended to improve Singapore's international cooperation regime – to make it clearer, smoother and more efficient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in line with our intent, as mentioned earlier, to take into account the varying practices of foreign countries, where processes for sealing or stamping may differ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As we continue to do so, we will ensure that robust safeguards are in place to ensure that Singapore will only act in meritorious cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With that, I conclude the first part of my speech on international criminal cooperation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I now turn to my next part on key changes to the trust regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will first explain the background of how trusts may be misused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will then detail how our legal regime aims to combat such misuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will end by going through the amendments that the Bill seeks to make to bolster our legal regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Generally, a trust is created when a person, the settlor, transfers legal title of certain identified property to another person, the trustee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The trustee is obliged to deal with that property for the benefit of another, the beneficiary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Trusts can be used for a wide variety of legitimate purposes, including succession planning, protection of vulnerable persons and charitable giving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, trusts can also be misused by criminals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: While the trustee is the legal owner of the trust assets, the trust assets are held for the benefit of the beneficiary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Trusts can thus be used to conceal the person who is ultimately entitled to benefit from the asset, particularly when they are used as part of a complex structure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As part of our three-pillar framework, we have enacted laws which require gatekeepers of the financial system, such as banks and other financial institutions, to obtain information as part of customer due diligence or CDD checks, thereby detecting and preventing misuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the customer is a trustee, the CDD checks should also be applied to persons with ownership or control over the trust, such as the settlor and the protector, as well as the beneficiaries, or persons who will benefit from the trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These CDD checks would include enhanced measures, such as checking on the source of funds for the settlor, in cases of higher money laundering or terrorist financing risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, if a law enforcement agency is conducting an investigation and wishes to find out more about the source of certain funds, and who the ultimate beneficiary is, their investigations would be facilitated if trustees are required to hold the relevant information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Thus, an obligation on trustees to hold such information complements the gatekeepers' CDD obligations and the powers of investigation of the law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The obligations imposed on trustees depends on the type of trust and their risk profile.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Some trustees, such as trust companies that are in the business of providing trust services professionally, are licensed and regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is to ensure that the trust companies adhere to high standards of integrity, professionalism and business conduct, and observe anti-money laundering and counter-financing of terrorism requirements similar to other financial institutions providing wealth management services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Trust companies may be involved in administering complex trust structures and dealing with high value assets and transactions, which exposes them to greater risk of being used for money laundering and other financial crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Trust companies' obligation to obtain and hold relevant information is found under the Trust Companies Act, the supporting subsidiary legislation and binding Notices issued by the MAS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The risk profiles of trustees that are not regulated by MAS are normally lower.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These lower risk trusts are typically not complex, as setting up a complex structure would typically require the assistance of professionals such as a trust company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To illustrate, a trust set up by an aged parent by transferring assets to a trusted family member to provide for a disabled child would fall under this category.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such trustees' obligations are generally found in the Regulations introduced under Part 7 of the Trustees Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments to the Trustees Act being moved today are primarily to Part 7 of the Trustees Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now turn to detail each of the key amendments to the Trustees Act: first, the scope of information which the trustees will need to obtain; second, an update to the sanctions for non-compliance with the obligations introduced under Part 7 of the Trustees Act; and third, on the powers to investigate trustees that breach their obligations introduced under Part 7 of the Trustees Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On the first point of the scope of information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Part 7 of the Trustees Act requires trustees to obtain and hold information on each person who is a "relevant trust party".

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes the settlor, the trustee, the beneficiaries and any person who has any power over the disposition of any property that is subject of the trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments to the Trustees Act will expand the scope of the information to be collected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With the amendments, the Trustee will now be required to collect the basic information of the trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes the identifier of the trust, for example, the name of the trust, or its tax reference number.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also includes the trust deed and the place where the trust is administered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The term "relevant trust party" will be expanded to include the "class of beneficiaries" and "natural persons exercising ultimate effective control over the trust".

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A "class of beneficiaries" refers to a group of individuals who are not yet known or identified in a trust instrument.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One example of a group may be the future descendants of the settlor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This information will usually be set out in the trust instrument which the trustees would likely have in their possession.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The trust instrument is the document setting out the terms of the trust and how the assets of the trust are to be managed or administered for the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: On the second point on sanctions for non-compliance, the Trustees Act currently provides that any contravention of the obligations introduced under Part 7 shall be punishable by a fine not exceeding S$1,000.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the maximum fines that may be imposed for comparable breaches in other pieces of legislation are higher.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the Accountants Act, as well as other pieces of legislation that this House has passed – the Companies and Limited Liability Partnerships (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act and the Business Trusts (Amendment) Act – the maximum fine for similar breaches is S$25,000.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With these amendments, the CTE and any authorised officers he may appoint will be empowered to investigate any breach of the trustees' obligations, introduced under Part 7 of the Trustees Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This transfer of investigative functions from the Police to MinLaw will develop MinLaw's subject matter expertise and allow investigators to more effectively address any breaches of the obligations introduced under Part 7 of the Trustees Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Beyond this, the CTE will also be empowered to issue codes of practice, guidelines or standards of performance if and when required.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These codes and guidelines or standards, if issued, will help to guide trustees of relevant trusts on how best to comply with their obligations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, the Bill needs examination to ensure we balance effective crime control with the rights of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I would like to raise several clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have concerns regarding privacy and safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that we balance international cooperation with our citizens' fundamental right to privacy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need strong assurances that the privacy rights of Singaporeans will not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, what is the plan for cooperating with non-prescribed foreign countries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While broad cooperation can be beneficial, it must come with reciprocity and robust safeguards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, how will the Government protect sensitive information shared with foreign authorities, ensuring it is used only for its intended purpose?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister of State outline these safeguards and explain how they will be enforced?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important that residents are informed if and when their information is shared, and that they have avenues for recourse if they believe their rights have been violated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it should not come at the expense of our residents' privacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Minister of State to address these concerns to alleviate the worries of Singaporeans and ensure that the right safeguards are in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What protections are in place for Singaporean and Permanent Resident customers when their financial data is requested by foreign entities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is considerable variation in data protection standards globally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that our citizens' financial data will be safeguarded, regardless of the requesting country?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There should be a clear and transparent process for residents to be informed of any data requests involving their accounts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ideally, they should have the right to contest these requests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans place great trust in our financial system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must not allow unchecked access to customer data by foreign entities to erode that trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents deserve assurances that their privacy and financial security are protected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, as Singapore is recognised as a safe haven for global investments, can the Minister of State confirm that our banks have the authority to refuse financial disclosures if complying would harm their reputations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to understand whether they can decline unjust requests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an issue that directly affects Singaporeans with assets or ties overseas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a review process to ensure that foreign orders are sound or even in line with our local laws?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This additional layer of protection could prevent disproportionate or unjust seizures originating from other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Supporting international justice is essential, but we must also safeguard Singaporeans from potentially unjust claims on their property.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Minister of State to address these concerns and confirm that the fundamental property rights of our citizens will not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have consistently advocated for stronger measures against financial crime, both inside and outside this House.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate the Government's firm stance demonstrated through recent Bills like the Anti-Money Laundering and Other Matters Bill and the Corporate Service Providers Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With each of these Bills, I have raised questions in Parliament regarding major financial crimes and our strategies for tackling them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tightening our laws, collaborating closely with international partners and enhancing due diligence are vital in today's landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Staying vigilant and proactive is our only means to ensure Singapore remains a trusted financial hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is why I am glad this Bill is being tabled.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It represents another critical step forward in our enforcement against complex financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I fully support our fight against cross-border crime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These issues are significant concerns for all Singaporeans, especially as criminals grow increasingly sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If implemented with care, these amendments will substantially bolster our enforcement efforts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we move forward, it is essential to uphold the delicate balance between justice and privacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Government will carefully consider my clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work together to build a system that not only strengthens our defences, but also respects and protects the rights of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only then we can truly create a secure, resilient and trusted nation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill before us further demonstrates the commitment of the Government and policing authorities to exhaust every effort in combating financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By aligning with the updated FATF recommendations, the Bill strengthens Singapore's position as a compliant and cooperative jurisdiction in the global fight against financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, can reinforce the country's position as a trusted financial centre, attracting investors and multinational corporations looking for a secure and transparent business environment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments also enable quicker and more effective cooperation in criminal matters with other nations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's capacity to support international law enforcement in asset confiscation, extradition and information sharing can make it a key player in global financial crime investigations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Stricter regulations on trustees and asset management enhance Singapore's defense against money laundering, promoting a stable and secure financial system.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must also acknowledge the challenges these changes may bring.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These sectors will face increased administrative and regulatory burdens, which could necessitate investment in staffing, technology and legal resources.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the balance between privacy and cooperation is another challenge we must carefully manage.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Heightened obligations to share information with foreign authorities may raise privacy concerns, particularly for clients who prioritise confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While we are committed to international cooperation, we must also ensure that we protect the data privacy of our clients to maintain Singapore's attractiveness as a financial hub.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the issue of international reciprocity.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: If other countries fail to uphold their side of the bargain, Singapore could find itself disproportionately bearing the burden of international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that these changes do not inadvertently push smaller players out of the market, as diversity in our financial ecosystem is essential to the continued growth of our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I have some clarifications for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: First, as international cooperation is critical for tackling cross-border crimes, how would Singapore streamline communication and operational procedures with foreign authorities to maintain swift collaboration?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Third, what processes and procedures can be implemented to address potential imbalances if other nations do not reciprocate Singapore's efforts in cooperation and resource allocation?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, clause 6 refers to providing assistance to non-prescribed foreign countries under certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would request clarification on the process the Attorney-General would use to verify compliance guarantees from these countries.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By fostering a transparent and secure financial environment, this Bill can increase confidence among international partners and clients.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I believe strengthening guidelines around the handling and transmission of sensitive information will require businesses to adhere more closely to best practices in data security, and help prevent breaches and supporting overall client confidence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I commend them for their advocacy to make sure that Singapore has a high bar, preventing it to be a place for financial crime and also, in relation to providing cooperation to other foreign jurisdictions in the fight against financial crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I will respond to address the questions that hon Members raised on the Bill, which relate to the topic of mutual legal assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip has raised concerns relating to privacy, confidentiality and transparency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I note that the pith of Mr Yip's questions is whether the MACMA and the amendments to it, strike the right balance between these concerns and the need for international cooperation in order to combat crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Parekh also raised similar queries, with specific emphasis on the processes and procedures for mutual legal assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When it comes to striking the right balance, we regularly grapple with such considerations when designing laws that confer powers over information and property belonging to private individuals and entities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the context of mutual legal assistance, it is critical that we do not, and indeed we will not, blindly accede to every request that we receive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: First, to address the general point about maintaining the right balance, I will broadly explain the existing safeguards set out in the MACMA, which ensures that the right balance is struck between the interests of the private individuals and entities on the one hand, and the demands of justice on the other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, I will further address Mr Yip and Mr Parekh's specific queries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But before turning to the safeguards in the MACMA and responding to the Members' queries, I would like to make a brief aside to address Mr Parekh's point about the compliance and operational costs in the trusts sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As stated earlier, the Trustees Act already imposes obligation on trustees to obtain and hold information on each "relevant trust party".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Insofar as the amendments also require the trustees to collect additional information, including the basic information of the trust, this information should be readily available from the existing documentation which the trustee will already have.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the first instance, section 19 of the MACMA sets out a list of requirements, such as a description of the offence and the relevant facts, that the foreign country must provide in order to make a request for assistance to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This ensures that every request will contain the relevant information that would enable the Singapore authorities to carry out a full assessment to determine if assistance can and should be granted in each case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Next, section 20 of the MACMA sets out several grounds under which assistance must or may be refused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This reflects the requirement of dual criminality, which generally applies to forms of assistance that are coercive in nature, including those seeking to obtain information or confiscate property from persons in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In other words, if the conduct in question would not have constituted an offence, had it occurred in Singapore, then we will not assist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Other examples where we must refuse assistance include: (a) where there are substantial grounds for believing that the request was made for the purposes of investigating, prosecuting, punishing or otherwise causing prejudice to a person on account of the person's race, religion, sex, ethnic origin, nationality or political opinions; or (b) where the thing requested is of insufficient importance to the investigation or could reasonably be obtained by other means; (c) there is also a general ground for refusal where it is contrary to public interest to provide the assistance sought.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These grounds for refusal, and many others that you will find in section 20 of MACMA, will ensure that we only act in meritorious cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our courts act as a final safeguard, including where the request pertains to the obtaining of information or confiscation of property of persons in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under the MACMA, the court has to be satisfied that the relevant legal requirements are met.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To summarise, Mr Speaker, Sir, MACMA contains robust safeguards, to ensure that assistance is provided only in meritorious cases, even as we seek to enhance our international criminal cooperation regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Parekh's first query was how Singapore would streamline communication and operation procedures with foreign authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Amending our laws and regulations would only go so far when interfacing with foreign authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Singapore regularly engages with our foreign counterparts, not only bilaterally, but also in multilateral and regional settings such as at FATF, the United Nations and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Singapore is also a member of informal networks, such as the Southeast Asia Justice Network, or SEAJust, which is a cooperation network that provides an informal platform facilitating direct contact and communication between central authorities for mutual legal assistance in criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As of 2024, there are 22 members to SEAJust, which go beyond those in Southeast Asia, such as Australia, China, France and the United States of America.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Such international engagements and networks allow us to share with other countries our respective laws, procedures and practices, including amendments such as those being considered today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This in turn creates a better understanding of each other's requirements and facilitates assistance both ways.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip and Mr Parekh asked how we cooperate with non-prescribed foreign countries, which are countries that we do not have a mutual legal assistance treaty with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also keep records of the foreign requests that we receive, including the undertakings that these countries provide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thus far, we have not encountered a situation where a foreign country has refused to honour its undertakings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip further asked about what recourse is available to persons affected by a foreign request, such as a production order or an application to enforce a foreign confiscation order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For production orders, Mr Yip may wish to note that under our laws, the person required to comply with an order may contest the order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the case of, for example, bank records to trace the movement of funds, the person or entity would be the bank.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As for confiscation orders, section 30 of MACMA provides that the Court must be satisfied that the person affected by the foreign confiscation order would at least have had the opportunity to defend himself in a foreign court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Third Schedule of MACMA further provides that the Court is not to exercise its powers to realise property in Singapore unless a reasonable opportunity has been given to persons holding any interest in the property to make representations to the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the same vein, our Bill will also provide that in cases where property is to be handed over to the requesting country, such persons must similarly be given a reasonable opportunity to make representations to the court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip also asked how the Government will ensure that sensitive information will be used only for its intended purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In a similar vein, Mr Parekh asked about the Attorney-General's powers and responsibilities in transmitting evidence to foreign authorities, along with safeguards for managing sensitive data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Attorney-General may also request that the thing requested would be returned upon completion of the criminal matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the course of assessing the request, the Attorney-General would ensure that the relevant undertakings are provided.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If they are not provided, the request would be refused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For instance, where it pertains to digital information, the foreign authority may be required to delete the information when it is no longer required for the criminal matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This provides Singapore with more options and greater control over the management of sensitive data, after it is handed over to the requesting authority.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Yip asked about safeguards that protect residents from unjust foreign confiscation orders and proposed to implement a cap or stricter criteria for enforcing foreign confiscation orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would first clarify that our foreign confiscation order regime would only affect assets located in Singapore and would not apply to assets located overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Next, I would reiterate that the MACMA contains robust safeguards, as well as stringent criteria – and I would also highlight that these are in line with international standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Furthermore, FATF recommends that powers that are available to domestic competent authorities should also be available for use in response to requests for mutual legal assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In other words, parity is key and it would be difficult to justify why a cap should apply to foreign confiscation orders, especially if this could constrain international efforts against money laundering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Once again, I thank the hon Members who have spoken and supported the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In summary, this Bill is about strengthening our regime for international cooperation, and our trusts framework.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It ensures, in line with our consistent approach for, prevention, detection and enforcement, that Singapore's processes for international cooperation remains relevant and effective, with robust safeguards, and that the misuse of trusts will be curtailed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.21 pm until 3.40 pm.
